lines.text: A trainer once tied a baby elephant to a wooden stake with a thin rope.
She pulled.
She cried.
She pulled until her leg ached.
The stake didn't move.
The whole camp watched. Nobody helped.
Day after day, the rope won.
Then one morning, she stopped pulling.
Years went by. She grew to three tons,
strong enough to push over a tree.
But she still stood beside that same small stake,
on the same thin rope.
One step would have pulled it out of the ground.
She never took it.
A traveller asked how a rope could hold her.
The trainer smiled. I don't hold her. Her memory does.
Psychologists call it learned helplessness.
In 1967, Martin Seligman and Steven Maier gave dogs shocks they could not stop.
Later, one jump over a barrier would have ended them.
Most of the dogs didn't even try.
Pain had taught them one rule: nothing I do matters.
You see it in classrooms, at work, at home.
The kid who failed once and stopped raising her hand.
The worker who stopped speaking up.
Half a century later, the same scientists found the twist.
Giving up is the brain's default. Control is what we learn.
So before you stop pulling, look at the stake.
It's smaller than you remember.
